extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper reports an acute COVID-19 treatment trial with Long COVID as an exploratory endpoint, not a trial enrolling participants with existing Long COVID. Treatment was a single IV infusion on day 0 during acute infection. Most outcome data reported as percentages without absolute event counts for EQ-5D-5L domains. Individual symptom frequency data (27 symptoms) available in figures (Fig 4) and supplementary tables (eTables 3-6) but not fully extractable from main text. SF-36v2 individual domain scores referenced as being in eTable 6 (p≥0.21 for all). Non-return to usual health reported as wRR=0.72 (95% CI 0.52-0.99) without IPW but the composite with death was wRR=0.65 (95% CI 0.48-0.89). AE data reported in prior publication (Evering et al. Ann Intern Med 2023) covering day 0-28 safety, not repeated in this Long COVID-focused analysis.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ACTIV-2) tested the monoclonal antibody combination amubarvimab/romlusevimab versus placebo in 780 high-risk, non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 10 days of symptom onset, enrolled January–July 2021. The primary composite outcome—long COVID at 36 weeks or hospitalization/death by 36 weeks—favored treatment (17% vs 24%, weighted risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.93), but this difference was driven entirely by fewer hospitalizations and deaths (4% vs 13%), not by any reduction in long COVID. Among participants who completed the symptom diary, long COVID prevalence was nearly identical: 16% in the treatment arm versus 14% in the placebo arm (weighted risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55), with no differences in symptom counts, severity, or quality of life at 36 weeks.

trial_rating.result_basis: The primary long COVID-specific outcome (death or long COVID composite) showed wRR=0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.27, p=0.55; long COVID prevalence was 16% (treatment) vs 14% (placebo), a null result.

summary: Ensitrelvir, an oral SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor, was tested against placebo in adults with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19 (Omicron variant) who were not sick enough to qualify for the main SCORPIO-SR trial. Among approximately 124–131 patients per arm, the proportion with long COVID symptoms at Day 337 was 3.5% (125 mg) and 3.4% (250 mg) versus 8.8% in the placebo group, representing roughly 60% risk reductions. For neurological symptoms specifically, risk reductions were 73% and 60% for the two doses versus placebo. This is a conference abstract with no p-values or confidence intervals reported, and the study was funded and largely staffed by Shionogi, the drug's manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Long COVID at Day 337: 3.5% (125 mg) and 3.4% (250 mg) vs 8.8% placebo; ~60% risk reduction stated, but no p-values or confidence intervals provided.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a 6-month follow-up study of the HENIVOT RCT, not a long COVID intervention trial per se. The population is ICU survivors of acute COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure assessed for long-term outcomes. The study design arm sizes differ between primary paper (N=54 helmet, N=55 HFNC randomized) and follow-up completion (N=35 helmet, N=36 HFNC). Note: Table 2 headers show N=31 helmet and N=33 HFNC for symptoms, N=30 each for pulmonary function, and N=35/N=36 for quality of life sections — these varying Ns are preserved in arm_results. The 30-s chair stand test p-value (0.65) is reported but no between-group effect size or CI is provided. The EQ-VAS high-flow group IQR in Table 2 has a formatting issue (value '[60-80]' appears on next line); extracted as median=70, IQR 60-80 based on text and table. Outcomes from Table 3 (intubated vs non-intubated subgroup) are captured in subgroup_analyses rather than as separate outcome entries to avoid duplication. Additional outcomes not extracted as separate objects due to space: maximal mid-expiratory flow 25-75 (MEF25-75), alveolar ventilation volume, residual volume/TLC ratio, FEV1<80% binary, FEV1/FVC<80% binary, TLC<80% binary, residual volume<80% binary, 6MWT interruption, 6MWT unable to walk predicted distance, various minor symptoms (dry cough, sore throat, rhinitis, smell disorder, taste disorder, dizziness, myalgia, chest pain, sicca syndrome, inappetence, diarrhoea, decreased visual acuity). Laboratory test results (hemoglobin, platelets, WBC, bilirubin, transaminases, creatinine, BUN, eGFR) reported in supplemental tables not available in main text.

summary: This pre-specified follow-up analysis of the HENIVOT randomized trial assessed 6-month outcomes in 71 ICU survivors with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure who had been treated with helmet noninvasive ventilation (NIV) or high-flow nasal oxygen. The primary outcome — the proportion of patients reporting any symptom at 6 months — did not differ between groups (90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71), and no significant differences were found in pulmonary function, physical performance, or quality of life between the two treatments. The only significant between-group difference was lower arthralgia in the helmet group (16% vs. 55%, p=0.002); separately, patients who required invasive mechanical ventilation during the acute illness had significantly worse pulmonary function and quality of life at 6 months regardless of initial treatment assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (proportion with any symptom at 6 months) showed no significant difference: 90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71, OR=1.67 (95% CI 0.36–7.65).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study has a complex design: the primary comparison is early (within 3 days) vs. late (after 3 days) antibiotic initiation (arm_id 1 vs 2, n=179 vs n=32), but the paper also extensively reports on vaccinated (n=59) vs unvaccinated (n=152) subgroups as quasi-arms (captured as arm_id 3 and 4 in outcomes 4-6). The paper is primarily about acute COVID-19 recovery, not long COVID per se — LC incidence is a secondary endpoint (21/211 = 10% overall). SpO2 data reported as means without SD for the early/late antibiotic comparison but with SD for vaccinated/unvaccinated comparison. The adjusted regression coefficient (b) for SpO2 by antibiotic timing from Table 5 (b=2.63, 95% CI 1.71-3.56) is extracted as an adjusted mean difference. The theoretical framework (SARS-CoV-2 bacteriophage behavior) is unconventional and the study has significant risk of bias due to non-randomized design, physician-directed treatment allocation, and heterogeneous antibiotic regimens.

Supplementary tables (referenced but not provided) likely contain additional per-arm and subgroup data. Forest plot figures (Figures 2 and 3) show additional subgroup aORs and mean differences that are partially described in text. summary: This single-arm longitudinal observational study followed 411 high-risk COVID-19 patients who received monoclonal antibody (mAb) infusion at a Federally Qualified Health Center in San Diego, assessing symptom burden and post-COVID conditions (PCC) at baseline, 14 days, and 28+ days (mean 72 days) post-symptom onset. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No control group; this is a single-arm observational study. PHQ-2 and PROMIS-29 D14 scores are described directionally in figures but not reported as exact means/SDs in tables — only D28+ means/SDs are in Table 3, so D14 values could not be extracted numerically. Symptom prevalences at D14 for the longitudinal subsample (N=199) are described narratively but exact percentages for all symptoms are only available from Figure 2 (not in table form); only selected values were extractable from text. Baseline prevalence for myalgia was stated as 38% in Discussion but not in a table. The between_group effects for the Poisson regression are labeled as risk_ratio (prevalence ratio) rather than adjusted_odds_ratio for Models 1 and 2 — these are all prevalence ratios from modified Poisson regression; the field 'adjusted_odds_ratio' was used as the closest schema match but these are actually adjusted prevalence ratios. Table 4 TTI chi-squared and t-test p-values are reported but without effect sizes per group, as the paper did not report per-TTI-group means/SDs for PROMIS or PHQ-2 outcomes.

summary: This single-center prospective cohort study examined 6-month pulmonary outcomes in 286 ICU survivors of critical COVID-19 requiring ventilatory support, comparing those who received corticosteroids per RECOVERY trial criteria (n=181) to those who did not (n=68, all from the first pandemic wave). Corticosteroid-treated patients had significantly lower DLCO % predicted at 6 months (mean 77% vs. 88%; adjusted MSD -8.3, 95% CI -14.2 to -2.4, p<0.05), though this fell just below the pre-specified 10% clinically significant threshold. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study examines corticosteroid treatment as an exposure rather than a prospectively randomized intervention; the comparison group (no corticosteroids) consists entirely of first-wave survivors, introducing substantial confounding by era and disease severity. Per-arm means for DLCO and RAND-36 are reported as mean with 95% CI rather than mean ± SD, so sd fields are null and ci_95_low/ci_95_high are used instead. The RAND-36 analysis had n=41 (no corticosteroids) and n=128 (corticosteroids) — slightly fewer than DLCO analysis. BMI medians with IQR are reported in Table 1 but no SD is given; BMI was not extracted as an outcome. The study period spanned March 2020–August 2021 with follow-up approximately 5–6 months post-ICU discharge. 37/286 enrolled participants had no data for either exposure group (neither corticosteroids nor no-corticosteroids per inclusion criteria — these are the excluded 'rescue treatment' cases per the flowchart; 68+181=249 of 286 total). p-values are stated only as <0.05 threshold, not exact values.

summary: This prospective cohort study assessed whether corticosteroid use during acute COVID-19 hospitalization (n=104 corticosteroid, n=202 no corticosteroid; predominantly dexamethasone 6mg/day for median 10 days) prevented persistent symptoms at 4 months post-admission in 306 discharged patients in France. In multivariable-adjusted logistic regression, corticosteroid use was not associated with having at least one persistent symptom (adjusted OR=1.00, 95% CI: 0.58-1.71, p=0.99) or with the number of persistent symptoms (adjusted IRR=1.04, p=0.74), with no significant association found for dyspnea or asthenia specifically. The null finding was robust across subgroups (ICU, ventilated patients) but the study is limited by confounding by indication as corticosteroid recipients had substantially more severe acute illness.

The forest plot (Figure 2) contains additional adjusted OR estimates for individual symptoms and subgroups but exact values for most are not reported in text; only asthenia (OR=1.33) and dyspnea (OR=0.82) are stated. summary: This prospective observational study compared PASC outcomes in 101 patients who received monoclonal antibody therapy (bamlanivimab or casirivimab/imdevimab) for acute COVID-19 versus 221 who received standard of care, followed for 6 months at a single US health system. mAb-treated patients had significantly fewer PASC symptoms at baseline (mean 1.06 vs 1.78, p=0.018) and 6 months (0.91 vs 1.75, p=0.043), and also had lower anxiety (GAD-7: 1.55 vs 3.49, p=0.034) and better baseline quality of life (EQ-5D index 0.842 vs 0.784, p=0.012). Both groups showed statistically significant within-group reductions in symptom burden over 6 months, with most between-group differences converging to non-significance by 6 months; however, the study did not adjust for substantial baseline confounders including time since infection, acute illness severity, and comorbidity differences.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined whether 30-day post-discharge prophylactic antithrombotic therapy (DOAC or dipyridamole) versus no treatment improved long-term outcomes in 1,746 adults hospitalized for moderate COVID-19 in Russia during 2020, with mean follow-up of 393 days. Both DOAC and dipyridamole were associated with markedly reduced all-cause mortality (0.6% and 0.7% vs. 5.9% in controls; p<0.001) and cardiovascular mortality, with effects persisting after propensity score weighting for baseline imbalances. DOAC significantly reduced stroke and pulmonary embolism, while dipyridamole reduced pulmonary embolism only; no significant differences in myocardial infarction or major bleeding were observed across groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weighted logistic regression results are reported as regression coefficients B (SE) rather than odds ratios; effect_value for propensity-weighted comparisons is therefore null as no OR/HR was directly stated. The note in the abstract that dipyridamole B=-17.95 (0.37) for cardiovascular mortality likely reflects a near-perfect separation (zero events in dipyridamole arm), making the coefficient unreliable. Control group had more historical/early-pandemic patients, creating a serious temporal confounding risk beyond measured covariates. Minor bleeding events could not be assessed due to study design. Some figures referenced in text (Figures 3-8) contain survival curves and event plots but no additional numeric data beyond what appears in Tables 2-3.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: LC prevalence was consistently lowest in AntiHm groups regardless of vaccination status; thrombosis reduction with antihistamines was significant in vaccinated and unvaccinated subgroups.

LC prevalence rose with successive infections in NoAntiHm group (0.5-10.2%); zero LC cases in AntiHm patients with ≥2 infections vaccinated before first infection, and zero in all AntiHm patients with ≥3 infections.
Thrombosis affected approximately 4% of patients over 60 across most CST centers; rising trend in both age groups.
59.3% of thrombotic events occurred in men; gender difference was statistically significant (p<0.0001).

summary: This retrospective population-based observational study from the Consorci Sanitari de Terrassa (n=192,651), Spain, compared long COVID incidence and thrombotic events in patients chronically prescribed antihistamines versus those not on antihistamines over five years (March 2020–March 2025). No long COVID cases were observed among antihistamine users with two or more SARS-CoV-2 infections vaccinated before first infection, and zero cases among those with three or more infections, though subgroup sizes were small and between-group comparisons did not reach statistical significance. Thrombotic events were significantly less frequent in antihistamine users across multiple polypharmacy strata and calendar years (overall 1.6% vs 3.3%, p<0.0001), with ORs ranging from 1.5 to 9.0 in individual annual/polypharmacy subgroup comparisons, and logistic regression confirmed an independent inverse association between antihistamine use and thrombosis after adjusting for age, sex, and number of chronic treatments.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper does not report per-arm denominators for annual thrombosis subgroup comparisons (Table 2 shows event counts per year and nT stratum, but not arm-level totals per year/stratum), so n_analyzed is null for outcomes 12-21. 2. The overall 1.6% vs 3.3% thrombosis rates cited in text appear to compare AntiHm with ≥1 nT vs NoAntiHm with ≥1 nT; the 3.3% figure is computed from 2,087 events/64,094 total (NoAntiHm ≥1 nT), making this a calculated inferred figure. 3. Many long COVID subgroup ORs cannot be calculated because AntiHm subgroups had zero cases (chi-square not applicable). 4. Detailed age and sex distributions per arm are in Supplementary File S0 (not available in main text); per-arm demographic data could not be extracted. 5. Logistic regression results are in Supplementary File S3 (not available); only the direction and significance (p<0.001 inverse association) are reported in text. 6. Several figures (Figures 1-4) show longitudinal event counts over time but exact per-trimester counts stratified by antihistamine use are not extractable from the figure descriptions — data described as 'only in figures' for year-by-year antihistamine comparisons not in Table 2. 7. The study covers both long COVID prevention and thrombosis reduction as co-primary outcomes; the paper is classified as an observational cohort/cross-sectional study of a fully enumerated population rather than a randomized trial.

summary: The Solidarity Finland trial randomized 156 hospitalized COVID-19 patients at 15 Finnish hospitals to oral imatinib 400 mg/day (up to 14 days) plus standard of care versus standard of care alone, with 1-year follow-up of mortality, recovery, quality of life, and long COVID symptoms. Imatinib showed no benefit on 30-day mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.23–5.07) or 1-year mortality (HR 1.34, 95% CI 0.46–3.88), and no significant difference in self-reported recovery (79% vs 88.3%, RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.78–1.06) or any EQ-5D-5L or symptom domain at 1 year. A meta-analysis of 4 trials (n=732) yielded a pooled mortality RR of 0.73 (95% CI 0.32–1.63), raising serious doubts about imatinib's benefit in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL: This is NOT a long COVID treatment trial. It is an acute COVID-19 early treatment trial (within 48h of symptom onset) that measured PASC symptoms at 90 days as a secondary outcome. The primary outcome is acute clinical deterioration. Viral load (Ct values) and cytokine data (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta) are presented only in figures (Fig 3a-e) without tabulated per-arm means and SDs in the main text; supplementary tables S1-S5 referenced but not available in extracted text. Very high differential attrition (86% retention in standard care vs 40-46% in treatment arms) raises major concerns about selection bias. The n_randomized per arm values were calculated by summing completed + withdrawn from Table 1/2 and do not perfectly add to 1900. The Day 14 and Day 28 standard care denominators appear to reflect only those still hospitalized/deteriorating, not the full cohort. The implausibly large effect sizes (0% deterioration in all treatment arms) and extreme PASC rates (99-100% in standard care) warrant caution. Paper was published in eClinicalMedicine (Lancet group). The 'n' column in the Niclosamide+Bromhexine row for Changes in vision appears to be a typo ('n' instead of '0').

Symptom prevalence data (Figure 4) is available only in figures, not extracted numerically. risk_of_bias.key_concern: This is not a randomized controlled trial but a decision tree simulation model with hypothetical uptake scenarios; all five RoB2 domains are not applicable, and findings are entirely model-derived estimates dependent on assumed inputs rather than observed experimental data.

summary: A Pfizer-funded decision tree model estimated the public health and economic impact of increased uptake of an additional dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech KP.2-adapted COVID-19 vaccine (2024-2025 formula) among US adults aged 65 and older. At the observed uptake of 8.9%, the model estimated the additional dose would prevent approximately 271,000 COVID-19 cases, 8,400 hospitalizations, 285 deaths, and 65,000 Long COVID cases annually, saving $623 million in direct medical costs. Raising uptake to 41.1% (matching initial dose uptake) was projected to avert nearly 39,000 hospitalizations and $2.8 billion in costs. This is a modelling study, not a clinical trial, and all authors are Pfizer employees or Pfizer-funded contractors, which is a significant conflict of interest.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is a conference abstract reporting a decision tree simulation model, NOT a randomized clinical trial or observational study of Long COVID patients. It does not study Long COVID treatment interventions — it models long COVID cases averted as one of several downstream outcomes of a vaccination uptake policy scenario. The paper is ineligible for inclusion in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. No per-arm baseline demographics, randomization, blinding, or clinical outcome data exist. summary: This multicenter open-label RCT (CAME-COVID study) tested clarithromycin (CAM) at 800 mg/day or 400 mg/day for 7 days versus standard care in 55 hospitalized Japanese adults with mild COVID-19 pneumonia not requiring oxygen. The primary endpoint — time to 50% reduction in a composite 7-symptom severity score — was not significantly improved in either CAM group versus control (trend only in the 800 mg arm, p=0.08). As a prespecified secondary endpoint, CAM 800 mg/day did significantly accelerate recovery from fatigue specifically (p=0.005), and also reduced several inflammatory and fibrotic cytokines; no serious safety concerns were attributed to CAM, though gastrointestinal and liver-related adverse events occurred exclusively in the 800 mg group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper primarily reports acute COVID-19 treatment, not Long COVID; the Long COVID relevance is that CAM 800mg/day significantly reduced fatigue (a key long COVID symptom) and fibrotic cytokines. Most cytokine data are only in figures (box plots) with no per-arm means/SDs reported in text or tables — only p-values for between-group comparisons extracted. Time-to-event (Kaplan-Meier) data for symptom improvement are only in figures; no median times or HRs reported. Chest radiography scores (Supplemental Table 2) not reported numerically in the main text. Serum IgA, IgG, IgM data are in Supplemental Figure 4 only. Complete blood count and other biochemical data (except eGFR, prothrombin time, blood sugar) not reported numerically. Baseline severity scores for control group note n=17, not n=18, for the days-from-onset/diagnosis variables. The allocation concealment method is not described. Per-arm AE counts are not provided numerically. Outcomes omitted due to data only in figures: complete symptom resolution (Kaplan-Meier, Figure 2B), time-to-improvement for headache/general unwellness/cough/shortness of breath/smell/taste disturbance (Figure 3B-G), oxygen therapy requirement (Supplemental Figure 1), serum immunoglobulins (Supplemental Figure 4), all other serum cytokines (Supplemental Figures 2-3).

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary composite symptom score improvement: CAM 800 mg vs control p=0.08 (non-significant); fatigue secondary endpoint p=0.005 but primary outcome was null.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Outcome 4 (rebound subanalysis) uses arm_id 3 (rebound) and arm_id 4 (no rebound) which are not defined in the main arms array — these are subgroups within the treated arm only. The overall cohort median age of 55 years and 66% female were reported for the full survey respondent sample (n=1611) not per arm. Days since COVID-19 in Table 1: treated 162±40 days, untreated 165±45 days — used to calculate follow-up of ~5.4 months. The paper states 5.4±1.3 months as mean±SD for follow-up in the abstract; the 1.3 months SD is noted but the days SD from Table 1 was used for arm-level estimates. Table 2 values appear transposed in the paper (columns labeled 'Not treated' and 'Nirmatrelvir treated' with totals 1378 and 233 respectively) — this appears to be a table formatting error in the manuscript; corrected values used are 1258 untreated (176 Long COVID, 1082 no Long COVID) and 353 treated (57 Long COVID, 296 no Long COVID) per the text.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Age 18-64: HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.75-0.91); Age ≥65: HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.76-0.86). Consistent protective effect across both age groups.
Female: HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.90); Male: HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.80-0.94). Both sexes showed protective benefit.
BMI <30: HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.85-0.99); BMI ≥30: HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.78-0.96). Both groups showed significant protection.
White: HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.78-0.89); Black/African American: HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.73-1.15, NS); Asian: HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.69-1.30, NS). Smaller sample sizes for minority groups limited power.
Hypertension subgroup: HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.99), significant protective effect.
Hyperlipidemia subgroup: HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.81-0.99), significant protective effect.
Type 2 diabetes subgroup: HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.80-1.02), not statistically significant.
Unvaccinated: HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.76-0.88); Vaccinated: HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.76-0.95). Protective effect observed regardless of vaccination status.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a propensity-score matched retrospective cohort study using TriNetX EHR data. The study examines long COVID defined as outcomes >90 days post-COVID-19 diagnosis (primarily stroke and mortality), NOT typical long COVID symptom burden (fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, etc.). Per-arm means/SDs not applicable — outcomes are time-to-event. Event counts and HRs extracted for all follow-up timepoints (overall, 6m, 12m, 24m). Pre-PSM non-Paxlovid group had n=1,425,792; post-PSM both arms had n=181,992. Table 1 had complex merged cells with pre/post PSM data interleaved — extraction focused on post-PSM values. Subgroup forest plot (Figure 3) extracted; note: vaccinated subgroup HR listed as '40.85' in table which appears to be a typographical error (should be 0.85 per text). Kaplan-Meier curves shown in Figure 2 but no raw numeric data extractable from curves beyond what is reported in Table 2. Adverse events not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective follow-up study, not an intervention trial. Age and sex demographics were reported for the overall sample and stratified by post-COVID vs non-post-COVID status only (not by drug exposure group), so baseline demographics were captured at the overall level only. COVID severity distribution: Low 43.1%, Low-medium 6.5%, Medium 19.5%, High 30.9% overall. p-values for combination drug OR results not reported in paper. Univariate analysis p-values: corticosteroids p=0.14, anticoagulants p=0.34, antibiotics p=0.96 (not significant for all).

Patients were frail outpatients at high risk of progression treated during acute infection (within 5-7 days of symptom onset). Long COVID outcomes assessed at 3 months. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cohort study examining whether acute in-hospital COVID-19 treatments (steroids, anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory agents, antivirals, or none) are associated with long-term outcomes 2 years post-discharge. The study found no significant associations for any outcome in either univariable or multivariable GEE analysis. Per-arm n_analyzed for each outcome not explicitly stated in Table 2 — only total n across all arms given (e.g., n=435 for recovery, n=460 for dyspnea, n=427 for FAS, n=432 for CFQ, n=432 for EQ-5D-5L, n=365 for 6MWT). Exact GEE effect sizes (ORs for binary, mean differences for continuous) with CIs were not reported in Table 2, only p-values. The 'n' in Table 2 header appears to refer to total analyzed, not per-arm. Percent female calculated as 100 minus percent male reported. BMI reported as medians with IQR in Table 1 but not transcribed as mean/SD. Univariable p-values also available: recovery 0.16, dyspnea 0.37, fatigue 0.44, CFQ 0.82, EQ-5D-5L 0.85, 6MWT 0.29.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational retrospective cohort study examining NMV-r for PREVENTION of PASC during acute COVID-19, not treatment of existing PASC. The abstract contains minor discrepancies in CI reporting between abstract (0.76-0.82 for broadly defined PASC 30-90d) and results text (0.77-0.83) and tables (0.767-0.827); table values used as most granular. Abstract OR for broadly defined PASC 90-180d reported as 0.25 (CI 0.23-0.29), but results text gives 0.67 (CI 0.64-0.69) and Table 3 gives 0.667 (0.643-0.693); abstract value appears to be a typographic error — table/results text values used. No baseline symptom/outcome data (study begins at acute COVID-19 diagnosis, not at PASC onset). E-values reported in tables for sensitivity to unmeasured confounding but no formal sensitivity analyses reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Study has two separate matched cohort analyses (A: SARS-CoV-2 vaccination n=1679/arm; B: influenza vaccination n=692/arm) treated here as four arms. The primary outcome metric is 'symptom burden' (days per week a symptom reported) but per-arm mean/SD values are NOT reported in tables — only event counts (n and %) for symptom prevalence and linear regression betas for burden change are provided. Between-group beta coefficients represent differential change in symptom burden days/week (vaccinated minus control). Table 3 reports beta coefficients for 29 symptoms for Analysis A; no equivalent table for Analysis B (null results). Survival analysis HR value not reported numerically — only log-rank p<0.005. Note: skin burning CI in Table 3 appears to have a transcription error (upper CI -0.40 instead of positive value); extracted verbatim. Additional symptoms with Table 2 prevalence data for Analysis A not separately structured as outcomes due to output size: headache, cough, dizziness, rhinorrhea, lack of appetite, brain fog, sneezing, sore throat, nausea, ophtalmodynia, rigors, hoarse voice, fever, abdominal pain, delirium, earache, lymphadenopathy, palpitations, rash, red welts. All Analysis B (influenza) symptom data in Table 5 shows no significant differences. BMI reported as median [IQR] not mean/SD.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Effect sizes for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir were generally consistent with primary analysis for patients >65 years. For patients ≤65 years, effect estimates differed from primary analysis with wide confidence intervals.
Similar results for male and female subgroups compared to main analyses in both trials.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This study is not a traditional long COVID treatment trial — it is a target trial emulation study examining antiviral treatment effects on cardiovascular post-acute sequelae in HOSPITALIZED COVID-19 patients. It has 4 study arms across 2 separate emulated trials (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir vs control; molnupiravir vs control), represented here as arms 1-4. Short-term (day 0-21) and long-term (day 22-365) outcomes are reported separately. Dysrhythmia, ischemic heart disease, and inflammatory heart disease in the molnupiravir short-term trial, and all long-term molnupiravir outcomes except cardiovascular mortality, were non-significant (outcomes 24 extracted; non-significant molnupiravir long-term outcomes for MACE, cerebrovascular, dysrhythmia, ischemic heart disease, inflammatory heart disease, other cardiac disorders, thrombotic disorders are not individually extracted as separate outcome objects to stay within size limits — their HRs range from 0.79-1.04 with p-values 0.09-0.93). Event counts for some outcomes from Fig 3 and Fig 5 forest plots — these were read from table data embedded in the figures. The long-term analysis denominators (arms 1/2: 14538/17723; arms 3/4: 9431/19469) differ from enrollment due to exclusion of patients who died or had events in first 21 days.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: ICU admission was significantly negatively associated with DLCO% at 3 months (coefficient -14.66, 95% CI -27.65 to -1.68, p<0.05) in adjusted analysis.
Presence of IgG antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 RBD at baseline was positively associated with DLCO% at 3 months (coefficient 13.54, 95% CI 6.17–20.90, p<0.001).
Higher viral load at hospital admission was significantly negatively associated with DLCO% at 3 months (coefficient -3.61, 95% CI -6.15 to -1.08, p<0.01).

Female sex was significantly negatively associated with both GGO >=10% (coefficient -1.56, 95% CI -3.21 to -0.24, p<0.05) and irreversible CT findings (coefficient -0.95, 95% CI -1.90 to -0.04, p<0.05).
History of smoking was significantly associated with CAT-score >= 10 at 3 months (coefficient 1.14, 95% CI 0.26–2.06, p<0.05).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an RCT sub-study focusing on 3-month pulmonary sequelae. The comparator structure is complex: remdesivir (n=16) vs its SoC (n=27); HCQ (n=40) vs its SoC (n=47). Some SoC participants served as control for both drugs simultaneously, so n=108 total does not equal sum of all subgroups. Arm 3 (SoC) represents the combined SoC pool; per-arm SoC group sizes differ by comparison (n=27 for remdesivir; n=47 for HCQ). The overall total population n=108 is used for biomarker and CT prevalence analyses. Biomarker outcomes (MMP-9, VEGF-A, SP-D, TIMP-2) are reported for the full cohort vs healthy controls (n=24) — healthy controls coded as arm_id=4 and full patient cohort as arm_id=5 for biomarker outcomes. IQR values for biomarkers not reported (medians only from figure caption). Reversible CT findings in Table 3 arm 1 vs arm 3 comparison shows 3 (18.8%) vs 4 (14.8%) but uses n values from remdesivir comparison. The coefficient estimate CIs for FEV1 comparisons appear to be t-statistics or standardised, not raw mean differences — reported verbatim as stated. KCO results also extracted in Table 2 but not given separate outcome object due to space — overall: median 97.4% (IQR 84.1–107.0); remdesivir 96.1 (78.1–99.8), HCQ 102.0 (92.0–108.0), SoC 92.8 (79.4–107.0). Mosaic pattern, reticular pattern, interlobular septal thickening, consolidations, and bronchiectasis CT findings are all in Table 2 but not given separate outcome objects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Retrospective cohort study comparing nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs. no antiviral treatment in non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Primary outcome is hospitalization at 28 days; secondary outcome is long COVID at 90 days — both are time-to-event outcomes analyzed via Cox regression. No per-arm means/SDs are applicable as outcomes are binary/time-to-event. Frequency of individual long COVID symptoms (fatigue 17.8%, muscle pain 12%, upper respiratory symptoms 8.2%) reported in Figure 2A but not broken down by arm. Kaplan-Meier curves shown in figures but numeric survival function values not tabulated. Adverse events explicitly noted as unable to determine due to retrospective design. The 'long COVID' outcome in this paper captures prevention of long COVID (acute treatment effect), not treatment of established long COVID.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study assessing nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for prevention of long COVID (taken during acute COVID-19, not as treatment of established long COVID). The primary outcome is binary (any long COVID symptom at 4 months). Forest plot of individual ORs shown in Figure 2 but exact OR values for non-significant symptoms not stated in text or tables — only p-values provided for those. The unadjusted primary outcome p-value is stated as 0.21 in abstract (44% vs 49.6%) but Table 2 shows 44% vs 50% with p=0.21; the 49.6% figure comes from 124/250. The n_screened of 11920 was calculated as 1162 (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir prescriptions) + 10758 (PCR-positive controls). Treatment duration inferred as 5 days (standard nirmatrelvir/ritonavir course). Follow-up of 4 months (120-150 days) equates to approximately 17-21 weeks; 17 weeks used as minimum. The paper reports percent_previously_hospitalized as 1% overall (5/500); 2 in treated arm, 3 in untreated arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study reports IPTW-adjusted risk ratios for the composite and 16 individual Long COVID outcomes. Exact RR values with CIs for each individual significant outcome are presented only in Figure 2 (not extractable from text — figures only); text confirms significance for: neuropsychiatric features, cognitive dysfunction, chest pain, cerebrovascular disease, thromboembolic disease, ischemic heart disease, diarrhea, headache, dysautonomia in overall population (all p<0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni). Per-arm event counts and percentages are not broken down by remdesivir exposure status in tables — Table 2 provides total n and rates per 100 person-years for ALL patients with ≥90 days follow-up pooled, not stratified by arm. Total follow-up: outcome assessment window is Day 90 to Day 270 post-admission = 180 days = ~26 weeks post-Day-90, or ~38.6 weeks total from admission. The 16 outcomes with nonsignificant results in overall population (dyspnea, fatigue, joint pain, cough, muscle pain, taste disturbance, smell disturbance) are reported but RRs only in Figure 2. Outcomes omitted from detailed extraction due to figure-only data: dyspnea/breathlessness, fatigue, joint pain/arthralgia, cough, muscle pain/myalgia, taste disturbance/dysgeusia/ageusia, smell disturbance/anosmia. Industry-funded study (Gilead Sciences, manufacturer of remdesivir); several authors are Gilead employees.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study examining interaction between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and COVID-19 vaccination on post-acute outcomes (mortality and rehospitalization). The study uses 4 exposure groups rather than a simple 2-arm design; arm_id=1 is the primary treatment group (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir + fully vaccinated), arm_id=2 is the reference group (no nirmatrelvir-ritonavir + not fully vaccinated), arm_id=3 is vaccination only, arm_id=4 is nirmatrelvir-ritonavir only. Between-group HRs are all vs. arm_id=2 (reference) unless otherwise noted. The paper also reports additive interaction statistics (RERI, AP, S) for the combined effect: for rehospitalization RERI=0.10 (95% CI 0.02-0.19, p=0.018), AP=0.07 (95% CI 0.01-0.12, p=0.017), S=1.26 (95% CI 1.02-1.55, p=0.032); for mortality RERI=0.28 (95% CI -0.001-0.55, p=0.051), AP=0.10 (95% CI 0.0007-0.20, p=0.048), S=1.19 (95% CI 0.99-1.43, p=0.070) — these additive interaction measures are not captured in the standard outcome structure. Subgroup results for age <65 years, males, and >6 months since vaccine dose are noted as in Supplement Tables without specific point estimates in main text. Follow-up ended 31 October 2023 or 1 year after discharge, whichever came first. Median days from nirmatrelvir-ritonavir prescription to positive PCR was 0 days (IQR 0-1).

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Protective effect of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir on PCC increased with age: ≥65y aHR 0.88 (0.87-0.90), 50-64y aHR 0.93 (0.92-0.95), 18-49y aHR 0.98 (0.97-0.99), 12-17y aHR 1.06 (0.66-1.13, NS).

In adults 50-64y and ≥65y, protective effect consistent across all CCI strata. In 18-49y, protective effect absent at CCI 0 (RR 1.00, p=0.674) but present at higher CCI scores. In adolescents, no consistent protective effect regardless of CCI.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a prevention study (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir given during acute COVID-19 to prevent long COVID), not a treatment study for established long COVID. Per-arm event counts for PCC by age subgroup are not reported in tables (only overall treated vs untreated). Detailed results for 45 individual conditions and 10 system categories are in Supplementary Tables 5 and 6, not provided in full text. Mean time to first PCC: treated 111 days/median 103 days; untreated 110 days/median 101 days. Table 2 provides unadjusted relative risk by CCI strata and age group — these have been noted in subgroup_analyses. CCI-stratified aHRs are not provided in the main text. The CI for the adolescent aHR appears anomalous in source text (0.66-1.13 for point estimate 1.06) — extracted verbatim. No adverse event data reported (observational claims study). Follow-up end date was 31 December 2022; index dates were 1 April–31 August 2022, giving a maximum follow-up of ~35 weeks but minimum 60 days (≈8.6 weeks) for PCC ascertainment.

Individual HR and 95% CI values for the 13 individual post-acute sequelae (outcomes 5-12 and ischemic heart disease, diabetes, dysautonomia, shortness of breath, cough) are reported only in Figure 3 — exact numerical values are not stated in the text or tables. Per-arm event counts for individual sequelae are not reported. The PASC score is not a traditional clinical outcome scale but a composite weighted burden metric. This is a prevention study (treatment given during acute COVID-19 to prevent long COVID), not a treatment study of established long COVID. The study population is veterans (>91% male, predominantly older, US-based), limiting generalizability. The paper is an observational cohort study using IPTW, not an RCT.

summary: This retrospective propensity-score-matched case-control study from Italy enrolled 737 adults with COVID-19 (January 2021–March 2022) to evaluate whether early treatment with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) or antivirals reduced the risk of long COVID (defined as symptoms persisting ≥4 weeks). In multivariable analysis, mAbs/antivirals were independently associated with reduced long COVID risk (OR 0.44, p=0.002), as was prior vaccination (OR 0.59, p=0.005); in propensity-score-matched analysis, long COVID occurred in 11% of treated patients versus 34% of untreated controls (p=0.001). The study concluded that both vaccination and early antiviral/mAb treatment significantly reduce the risk of developing long COVID.

summary: This retrospective cohort study from Vietnam compared standard of care (SoC) alone versus SoC plus antivirals (predominantly molnupiravir) in 142 vaccinated adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 breakthrough infection. Antiviral use was associated with numerically lower rates of residual respiratory symptoms >7 days (20.3% vs 27.9%) and long COVID-19 (8.1% vs 11.8%), but neither difference was statistically significant (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.22-1.20, p=0.12 and OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.16-1.90, p=0.35, respectively). Subgroup and sensitivity analyses also showed no significant benefit of antivirals, suggesting these agents should not be routinely prescribed for breakthrough COVID-19 prevention of long COVID in vaccinated, lower-risk populations.

summary: This retrospective observational cohort study used N3C electronic health records from 302,626 US adults with depression and COVID-19 (September 2021–December 2022) to evaluate whether SSRI use during acute COVID-19 reduces subsequent 12-month Long COVID risk. After aggressive nonparametric confounder adjustment using targeted maximum likelihood estimation and Super Learner, SSRI users showed a significantly lower risk of Long COVID compared to nonusers (adjusted RR 0.922, 95% CI 0.863–0.986), with a similar result in new SSRI users (aRR 0.886, 95% CI 0.780–0.985). Individual SSRI drug subtypes all showed protective point estimates but none were individually statistically significant, and no dose-response relationship was detected for fluoxetine.

summary: This retrospective cohort study examined the short- and long-term effectiveness of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus molnupiravir in 1,745 Hong Kong asthma patients infected with COVID-19 (Omicron era), using SMR weighting to adjust for confounding. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with significantly reduced risks of acute mortality (HR 0.27), post-acute mortality (HR 0.49), all-cause post-acute hospitalization (HR 0.72), and myocardial infarction (HR 0.10) versus no antiviral; molnupiravir reduced only acute mortality versus no antiviral. Head-to-head comparison showed nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was superior to molnupiravir for post-acute all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.65, p<0.001) and asthma exacerbation in moderate-to-severe asthma patients, suggesting nirmatrelvir/ritonavir offers broader post-acute protection in the asthma population.

All outcomes are time-to-event (Cox HR); no continuous means/SDs are available. The denominator n values for cause-specific hospitalization outcomes differ from total enrolled because patients with prior history of the condition were excluded from those analyses. Subgroup HR values for ICS strata were reported in text without CI for some comparisons. Adverse events not systematically reported. Median follow-up was 365 days (IQR 335-365).

summary: This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US EHR platform examined whether SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced long COVID risk in 5,162 matched pairs of adults with type 2 diabetes who contracted COVID-19 between 2020-2024. SGLT2 inhibitor users had a significantly lower risk of developing long COVID over 12 months (HR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91), with particularly pronounced reductions in anxiety/depression (HR=0.73), headache (HR=0.56), cognitive symptoms (HR=0.69), pain (HR=0.84), and abdominal symptoms (HR=0.84); fatigue, chest pain, abnormal breathing, and myalgia were not significantly reduced. The protective association was consistent across age groups and sexes and was replicated in three sensitivity analyses comparing SGLT2i to DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective cohort study — not an interventional trial. Outcomes are ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes (incident long COVID diagnoses), not patient-reported symptom scales, so no per-arm means/SDs are available. All quantitative results are event counts and Cox hazard ratios. The post-COVID-19 condition category (unspecified) HR=0.81 (95% CI 0.42-1.56, n=16 vs 20 events) was not extracted as a separate outcome given the very small event count and wide CI. Kaplan-Meier curves were presented in figures; exact numerical incidence rates from those curves not reported in text. The discussion section mentions HR=0.94 (95% CI 0.87-1.00) and HR=0.92 (95% CI 0.84-1.00) for 'overall HRs' but these appear to contradict the forest plot values and may refer to a different time window or unadjusted analysis — not extracted to avoid confusion. No adverse events were reported.

summary: This prospective cohort study followed 222 COVID-19 survivors discharged from a single hospital in Saudi Arabia at a median of 122 days post-discharge to assess post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS). Among all patients, 56.3% reported persistent symptoms (primarily dyspnea 40%, fatigue 30%, cough 28%) and 28.8% had not returned to their pre-COVID baseline. In multivariable analyses, treatment with interferon β-1b-based triple antiviral therapy during hospitalization was significantly associated with lower risk of persistent symptoms (aHR 0.28, 95% CI 0.14-0.57) and lower odds of non-return to baseline (aOR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04-0.75), though treatment was physician-decided and not randomized, limiting causal inference.

summary: This EHR-based target trial emulation used the N3C database (445,738 patients with COVID-19 eligible for Paxlovid from April 2022-February 2023) to estimate whether Paxlovid treatment during acute COVID-19 prevents long COVID (PASC) onset. Paxlovid had no significant effect on overall PASC incidence (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02) or respiratory symptoms, but showed small statistically significant protective effects on incident cognitive (RR 0.91) and fatigue (RR 0.94) symptoms. Stratified analyses identified small protective effects in patients aged ≥65 years (RR 0.92, NNT 233) and with CCI 3-4 (RR 0.83, NNT 76), but the authors conclude Paxlovid is unlikely to be a definitive solution for PASC prevention given the negligible absolute effect sizes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a PASC prevention study (Paxlovid given during acute COVID-19), NOT a treatment study for established long COVID. Study period: April 1, 2022 to February 28, 2023 (mostly Omicron BA and later subvariants). The pooled sequential trial cohort of 460,803 records differs from the 445,738 unique patients due to sequential trial design allowing some patients to appear in both treatment and control groups across different trials. Age data reported only as distributional bins (not means/SDs). Cumulative incidence values in Table 3 are reported as proportions (e.g., 0.045 = 4.5%). Death counts: Paxlovid arm 157 deaths (29-180 days), 51 deaths (1-28 days); control arm 609 deaths (29-180 days), 366 deaths (1-28 days). Extensive sensitivity analyses (14 variations) all confirm null primary result — see Table 3. Also note: the paper reports adjusted cumulative incidence estimates (4.53% treated, 4.60% untreated) in text but the raw (unadjusted) event counts show 4.4% treated vs 4.1% untreated, reflecting the IPTW adjustment. Vaccination subanalysis: 115,823 patients, 8 sites, 79.15% fully vaccinated, 45.67% treated. Doubly robust adjustment gave HR 0.983 (95% CI 0.950-1.018, p=0.305).

summary: This propensity score-matched longitudinal cohort study from Indonesia examined whether favipiravir (an antiviral given during acute COVID-19) reduced the incidence of post-COVID depression in 712 participants followed biweekly for 60 days. Depression occurred in 16.0% of favipiravir recipients versus 21.1% of non-recipients; after adjustment for multiple confounders using Cox regression, favipiravir was associated with a significantly lower hazard of post-COVID depression (aHR 0.488, 95% CI 0.339–0.701, p<0.001). Favipiravir showed specific protective effects against depressive mood (aHR 0.378) and anhedonia (aHR 0.543), but not sleep disorders, concentration disturbance, or fatigue; living alone was independently associated with greater anhedonia risk.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. 1) The paper uses Cox regression and reports adjusted estimates labeled as 'aOR' in the text and 'Exp(B)' in Table 3, but since it uses Cox regression, these are properly hazard ratios (aHR), not odds ratios — extracted as adjusted_hazard_ratio accordingly. 2) Per-arm sample sizes (356 per arm) are inferred from the 1:1 matching of 712 total participants and the reported depression event counts (57/356 favipiravir, 75/356 non-favipiravir). 3) Symptom-specific PHQ-9 subscale analyses for sleep disorders (S7 Table), concentration (S8 Table), and fatigue (S9 Table) are referenced as supplementary tables but no numeric estimates are provided in the main text; only depressive mood and anhedonia HR values are in the main text. 4) No per-arm means/SDs for PHQ-9 total scores are reported — only binary event counts and HRs. 5) Vaccination percentage of 52.5% for favipiravir arm and 47.5% for non-favipiravir arm represents those NOT infected within 14 days of second vaccine dose (i.e., vaccine-protected group).

summary: This retrospective cohort study used N3C electronic health record data from 74 US institutions (October 2021–April 2023) to compare incident PASC risk among T2DM adults on prevalent monotherapy metformin (n=5,596) versus sulfonylurea or DPP-4 inhibitor (n=1,451), using entropy balancing for confounding control. In the weighted analysis with ICD-10-defined PASC, 3-month and 6-month risk ratios were 0.86 (95% CI 0.56–1.32) and 0.81 (95% CI 0.55–1.20), respectively — directionally consistent with benefit but not statistically significant. The authors conclude that the results are compatible with a reduced PASC risk with metformin but that wide confidence intervals and methodological limitations (prevalent-user design, non-specific outcome definition) preclude causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study uses two cohorts: cohort one (n=7,047; 29 sites) for ICD-10-defined PASC outcome; cohort two (n=13,824; 37 sites) for ML-predicted probability outcome. The 'percent female 56%' stated in abstract refers to overall cohort; arm-level percent female is calculated as 100 minus percent male (44.0% male in metformin arm, 45.9% male in SU/DPP4i arm). Risk difference for 3-month ICD-10 outcome in abstract states -3.06 per 1000 (approx -0.31 per 100) which matches Table 4; similarly 6-month RD -4.91 per 1000 ≈ -0.49 per 100. summary: This large observational cohort study using target trial emulation analyzed 497,499 SARS-CoV-2-infected adults from 29 US PCORnet EHR repositories to assess whether nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) prescribed within 5 days of infection reduces Long COVID risk. Among high-risk non-hospitalized adults (n=431,707 analyzed), Paxlovid was associated with significantly reduced incidence of Long COVID (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.87-0.89; absolute risk reduction 2.99 events/100 persons), all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.70), and death (HR 0.53) in the 30-180 day post-acute period. No significant Long COVID risk reduction was observed in low-risk patients (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11), suggesting Paxlovid's preventive benefit for Long COVID is limited to high-risk individuals.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study in Spain followed 1,966 patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) over 12 months after acute COVID-19 infection to identify risk factors for post-acute sequelae (PASC) and evaluate the impact of acute-phase treatments. subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Younger patients (age group 30) recovered quicker than older patients (50-65), p<0.001 in Cox regression, but HR=0.963 (below meaningful significance); no statistically significant difference in protocol response by age group.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: COVID score and time to recovery
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both groups responded similarly in first 5 days; from day 5 onward healthy patients improved faster than MS patients. Cox HR=1.003 (p=0.988), not statistically significant.
LRS patients recovered slower than GS patients (mean 13.083 vs 11.862 days); Cox HR=0.688, 95% CI 0.493–0.961, p=0.028, statistically significant.

Statistically significant difference across severity groups (log-rank Chi-square=188.972, p=0.000); mean recovery times were 10.0, 11.965, and 13.062 days for mild, moderate, and severe, respectively.

summary: This uncontrolled single-arm prospective observational study enrolled 183 adults with acute PCR-confirmed COVID-19 (Feb 2020–Jun 2022) from multiple countries, and evaluated a multi-component protocol including probiotics, vitamins D/C/E, zinc, selenium, glutathione, N-acetylcysteine, quercetin, and a low-carbohydrate diet, with pain killers as the only permitted medication. COVID symptom scores decreased significantly from a mean of 7.66 (SD 1.26) at baseline to 6.39 (SD 1.12) at 72 hours (p<0.005), with a regression-modeled daily reduction of 0.97 score points (R²=0.97, p<0.0001); overall median recovery was 13 days, shorter than historical comparators of 12–21 days. The study had no control group and was primarily aimed at preventing long COVID rather than treating it; the authors reported no long-term post-COVID complications at 6-month follow-up, but this claim cannot be evaluated without a comparator group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. IMPORTANT CLASSIFICATION NOTE: This is NOT a long COVID treatment study — it is an acute COVID-19 management study aimed at PREVENTING long COVID. Participants had active, not post-acute, COVID-19 infection. The paper should potentially be excluded from a long COVID treatment meta-analysis. The study lacks a control group; all subgroup comparisons (healthy vs MS, GS vs LRS, severity groups) are internal subgroups of the single intervention cohort, not separate arms. Baseline COVID score for mild (mean=5.0, SD=0.0) and moderate (mean=6.63, SD=0.52) and severe (mean=8.48, SD=0.67) groups extracted from Table 1. Some data are only in figures (daily COVID score trajectories by subgroup, Kaplan-Meier curves) — only summary statistics from tables and text were extractable. The Cox regression HR for age is per-year (HR=0.963, p<0.001, 95% CI 0.944–0.983), not per age group. Ethics approval was explicitly not obtained for this study.

summary: This retrospective population-based cohort study of 188,532 Singaporeans aged ≥60 years with SARS-CoV-2 infection examined whether early outpatient nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment (n=10,905) reduced risk of postacute sequelae compared to untreated controls (n=177,627), using overlap-weighted competing-risks regression on national registry and claims data. No statistically significant reduction in any prespecified postacute outcome was observed at 31–180 days post-infection, including composite sequelae (aHR 1.06; 95% CI 0.94–1.19), MACE (aHR 0.80; 0.61–1.06), cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, or autoimmune complications, or any symptom-based sequelae (aHR 0.97; 0.80–1.18). The authors attribute the null finding largely to a highly vaccinated/boosted cohort (95% with ≥3 doses) and a very low hospitalization rate (<2%), which may have left little additional benefit for antivirals to confer.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Detailed per-arm event counts and incidence rates for individual outcomes are not reported in the paper text — only adjusted hazard ratios with 95% CIs are provided. Baseline demographic details by arm (age mean/SD, % female) are referenced as appearing in Table 1 but not reproduced in the text. Full Table 2 (individual outcome HRs) and Tables S1–S16 (subgroup analyses) are referenced but not included in the provided text. The follow-up period of mean 149.68 days (SD 5.63 for untreated; 5.38 for treated) was reported. Total follow-up of 180 days calculated as 25.7 weeks. Treatment duration inferred as 5-day course (0.71 weeks) per standard nirmatrelvir/ritonavir protocol. Outcome data for individual symptom-based outcomes (palpitations, chest pain, cough, dyspnoea, headache, joint pain, anosmia, memory problems) are present in Table 2 but only the composite aHR is available in the text; individual symptom HRs not extractable from the provided text.

summary: This nationwide retrospective propensity-score-matched cohort study in South Korea examined whether oral antiviral treatment (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or molnupiravir) during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in adults aged ≥60 years diagnosed during the 2022 Omicron wave. Among 957,036 matched pairs for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and 243,360 matched pairs for molnupiravir, both antivirals were significantly associated with reduced incidence of multiple PASC outcomes (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, neurological, gastrointestinal, and metabolic) between 30 and 120 days post-diagnosis, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showing broader and larger risk reductions (e.g., aHR 0.57 for new dialysis) compared to molnupiravir.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Full numeric data for all 27 PASC outcomes across both cohorts are in Tables 2 and 3 (not available in this text excerpt — supplementary tables eTables 3-30 also not available). Only outcomes explicitly reported with HR and 95% CI in the main text were extracted here. The asthma nirmatrelvir/ritonavir CI (0.83-0.94) appears internally inconsistent with the stated aHR of 0.98 — this may be a typographical error in the paper; values extracted verbatim. The acute renal failure CI (0.78-0.82) is also inconsistent with aHR 0.85 — likely a transcription error in the paper text; extracted verbatim. Per-arm event counts and raw rates were not reported in the available text. CCI mean reported as 2.03±1.91 (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) and 2.53±2.11 (molnupiravir) groups but not per arm separately for treated vs matched controls. Age described as mean 72-73 years across cohorts but exact per-arm values not explicitly stated.
